name: Electric Field Concepts
what: This subtopic covers the definition of an electric field as a vector field, the rules for drawing electric field line diagrams around point charges and between parallel plates, and the distinction between electric monopoles and dipoles. It also covers how electric fields compare to gravitational fields.
why: The field model is the conceptual foundation for all electric force and energy calculations. Understanding how to draw and interpret field line diagrams is a required practical and exam skill, and distinguishing monopoles from dipoles connects electric fields to both magnetic fields and real-world molecular structures.

items.title: I can describe what an electric field is and explain why it is classified as a vector field
items.what: An electric field is a region of space where a charged particle experiences an electric force. It is a vector field because at every point it has both a magnitude (field strength in N C⁻¹) and a direction, defined as the direction of the force on a small positive test charge placed at that point.
items.why: The vector nature of electric fields means that both magnitude and direction must be specified in any description or diagram. By convention, the direction is defined using a positive test charge, which is a standard that must be applied consistently in all field line diagrams and calculations.
items.example: At a point 0.10 m to the right of a positive charge, the electric field has a magnitude of 1.8 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ and points radially outward (to the right). Both the value and the direction are needed to fully describe the field at that point.

items.title: I can draw and interpret electric field line diagrams for a single positive charge and a single negative charge
items.what: For a single positive charge, electric field lines point radially outward in all directions. For a single negative charge, field lines point radially inward toward the charge. In both cases, field lines are more densely packed closer to the charge, indicating a stronger field, and spread out further away.
items.why: Drawing and reading field line diagrams is a core practical and exam skill. The density of lines conveys field strength, and the direction of arrows conveys the force direction on a positive test charge — both are assessed in VCAA examinations.
items.example: A diagram for a +Q charge shows arrows pointing outward like the spokes of a wheel, with the arrows closer to the charge drawn more densely packed. A diagram for a −Q charge has the identical pattern of lines but with all arrows reversed, pointing inward.

items.title: I can draw and interpret electric field line diagrams for two charges and for parallel plates
items.what: For two opposite charges (a dipole), field lines curve from the positive charge to the negative charge. For two like charges, field lines repel each other and no lines connect the two charges. Between two oppositely charged parallel plates, field lines are straight, parallel, and evenly spaced, representing a uniform field.
items.why: These three configurations appear regularly in VCAA exam questions. The parallel plate case is especially important because it is the basis for all uniform field calculations involving F = qE and W = qV.
items.example: For a +Q and −Q charge placed near each other, field lines leave the positive charge, curve through the space between them, and terminate on the negative charge. Between two oppositely charged parallel plates, the field lines run straight from the positive plate to the negative plate with equal spacing throughout.

items.title: I can state the rules for drawing valid electric field line diagrams
items.what: Electric field lines must run from positive charges to negative charges. They must leave and arrive at conducting surfaces at 90 degrees. Field lines can never cross each other, because crossing would imply the field points in two directions simultaneously at the same point, which is physically impossible.
items.why: Drawing field lines that violate these rules is a common exam error. Understanding why each rule exists (particularly the no-crossing rule) demonstrates deeper conceptual understanding and is rewarded in extended response questions.
items.example: A student draws a field line diagram where two lines cross near a positive charge. This is incorrect: at the crossing point, the field would need to point in two directions at once, which cannot happen. The correct diagram shows lines that curve apart and never intersect.

items.title: I can explain the difference between an electric monopole and an electric dipole
items.what: An electric monopole is a single isolated charge — either positive (field lines pointing outward) or negative (field lines pointing inward). An electric dipole consists of two equal and opposite charges separated by a short distance, with field lines running from the positive charge to the negative charge.
items.why: The monopole/dipole distinction is part of the study design glossary and connects to comparisons with gravitational fields (mass is always a gravitational monopole) and magnetic fields (magnetic dipoles have no monopole equivalent). It also has real-world relevance in molecular chemistry.
items.example: A single electron is an electric monopole — its field lines all point inward. A water molecule (H₂O) behaves as an electric dipole because oxygen pulls shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen does, creating a partial negative charge on the oxygen end and partial positive charges on the hydrogen ends.

items.title: I can distinguish between uniform and non-uniform electric fields, and identify electric fields as static or changing
items.what: A uniform electric field has constant strength and direction at all points, represented by evenly spaced parallel field lines. A non-uniform field varies in strength and direction. A static field does not change over time; the fields between charged parallel plates and around stationary point charges are both static.
items.why: These classifications appear directly in the study design and in exam questions. Knowing whether a field is uniform or non-uniform determines which formulas apply, and distinguishing static from changing fields connects this topic to electromagnetic induction studied later.
items.example: The electric field between two parallel charged plates (with fixed charge) is uniform and static — the field lines are parallel and do not change over time. The electric field around a single point charge is non-uniform and static — it is strongest close to the charge and weaker further away, but it does not change unless the charge moves.
